UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF THE JOINT CONSUMER ADVOCATES 
Pursuant to section 313 of the Federal Power Act (FPA)1 and Rule 713 of the 
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission or FERC) Rules of Practice and 
Procedure,2 the Delaware Division of the Public Advocate, District of Columbia Office of 
People’s Counsel, Illinois Citizens Utility Board, Office of the Illinois Attorney General, 
Maryland Office of the People’s Counsel, and New Jersey Division of Rate Counsel 
(collectively, Joint Consumer Advocates) respectfully request rehearing of PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C., 196 FERC ¶ 61,245 (2026) (RBP Order or Order).  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (PJM) underlying Reliability Backstop Procurement 
(RBP) proposal is meant to enable the procurement of sufficient “new capacity to address 
significant resource adequacy challenges primarily driven by an influx of large loads.”3 
The proposal, however, is fundamentally flawed because it permits the unmitigated 
exercise of seller-side market power and its design seems guaranteed to ensure that PJM 
procures more resources than are necessary, at costs higher than are warranted.4 
Notwithstanding the Commission’s concerns with several aspects of the proposal, the 
 
1 16 U.S.C. § 825l.  
2 18 C.F.R. § 385.713. 
3 RBP Order P 1.  
4 See, e.g., Protest, Motion to Reject, and Alternative Request for the Imposition of Conditions of Joint 
Consumer Advocates at 5-7 (Aug. 21, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260821-5183 (JCA Protest).

- 2 - 
 
Commission accepted without alteration many deeply flawed components of the proposed 
RBP framework. In doing so, the Commission erred in numerous respects and failed to 
meet its statutory obligation to protect PJM’s already over-burdened ratepayers from unjust 
and unreasonable charges.  
First. The Order accepts RBP without requiring reasonable market power screens 
or mitigation,5 while acknowledging (1) that the RBP’s pay-as-bid structure makes it 
“theoretically less likely [that sellers will] offer near their marginal costs,”6 and (2) PJM’s 
admission that sellers are instead more likely to offer the expected clearing price.7 In doing 
so, the Order ignores over 50 years of judicial and Commission precedent that permits the 
use of market-based transactions to set just and reasonable rates under the FPA only where 
there will likely be fair competition based upon marginal cost bids and adequate mitigation 
of seller-side market power. The Order assumes without evidence that mitigation measures 
are unnecessary because: (1) the exercise of market power will be averted if sufficient 
resources choose to participate in the RBP  and drive down prices, and (2) the inclusion of 
a proposed megawatt (MW)-weighted average-price cap will “discipline[] costs.”8 But, as 
shown below and as set forth in the JCA Protest, these assertions are legally insufficient, 
factually unsupported, and at odds with the record evidence.  
Second. The Order accepts a price cap of $555/MW-day, on a MW-weighted 
average basis, finding, without reasoned explanation, “that using the $555/MW-day price 
 
5 RBP Order P 75.  
6 Id.  
7 PJM, Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from New 
Load Adjustments, Transmittal at 71 & n.184 (July 31, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260731-5214 (PJM Filing) 
(quoting id., Attach. C, Affidavit of Ms. Danielle Croop ¶ 33 (Croop Aff.)). 
8 RBP Order P 98.

- 3 - 
 
cap for the 2028/2029 [Base Residual Auction (BRA)] . . . is a reasonable proxy of load’s 
maximum willingness to pay for RBP capacity.”9 The Order ignores Joint Consumer 
Advocates’ arguments demonstrating that the BRA is not analogous to the RBP and that a 
$555/MW-day average price cap is unjust and unreasonable in the RBP context:  
• 
The BRA is a single-clearing-price auction that structurally incentivizes 
suppliers to offer capacity at the supplier’s marginal cost. In that context, a 
market price cap is a second-line protection against unjust and unreasonable 
prices. In the RBP pay-as-bid structure, the incentive to offer at marginal 
cost is missing, and the market average price cap affords bidders the ability 
to exercise market power by gaming their bids around the price cap. And 
whatever prices are set in the RBP will apply for a much longer period. It is 
essential to ensure that any RBP price cap is set at an appropriate level to 
ensure just and reasonable rates. 
• 
The BRA sets capacity auction clearing prices for commitment periods of a 
single year, offering little long-term price certainty. In contrast, the RBP 
sets prices for terms up to 15 years. As both PJM and FERC acknowledge, 
greater price certainty reduces supplier risk and costs.10 RBP’s greater 
revenue certainty therefore argues for a lower price cap in the long-term 
RBP than the cap that applies in the annual, single-year BRAs. 
• 
The $555/MW-day is borrowed from Point 1 of the Variable Resource 
Requirement (VRR) curve that would have applied in the BRA for the 
2028/2029 Delivery Year but for PJM’s request and the Commission’s 
approval to apply a temporary price collar with a lower cap. While Point 1 
of the VRR is a reference cost grounded in the estimated levelized Cost of 
New Entry (CONE) for a combustion turbine (CT) reference resource,  the 
RBP has no reference resource or VRR curve and there is no evidence that 
a $555/MW-day price cap will reflect the production costs of the resources 
that the RBP will procure. 
• 
The RBP proposal borrowed a BRA price cap that was not in effect for the 
2028/2029 Delivery Year because it was replaced by price collar with a 
lower cap. As the Order acknowledges, that cap—accepted by the 
Commission as just and reasonable—was just $325/MW-day.11 The Order 
fails to explain how it also could be just and reasonable to accept an RBP 
 
9 Id. P 74. 
10 See id. P 76 (“As PJM explains, long contract terms create revenue certainty for RBP Resources and 
generally can reduce financial and development risk and may improve financing opportunities through 
lower capital costs or more favorable financing terms.”). 
11 Id. P 13.

price cap that is 70% higher and will be applied to commitment periods up 
to 15 times longer than was the case for the 2028/2029 BRA.     
Third. The RBP Order accepts without explanation the requirement that resources 
procured through the RBP be subject to a 15-year commitment despite PJM’s admission 
that a resource procurement “of at least five years is capacity that will address the reliability 
shortfall.”12 The Order acknowledges but fails to address Joint Consumer Advocates’ 
argument that it is “unjust and unreasonable to charge ratepayers for the acquisition of 
years of capacity that is not needed to address the reliability shortfall and serves no cost-
efficiency or other economic purpose.”13 The Order’s acceptance of RBP’s 15-year 
procurement terms could unjustly and unreasonably saddle captive ratepayers with some 
$13 billion in excessive and unnecessary RBP costs. 
Fourth. Finally, the RBP Order is arbitrary and capricious because it fails to engage 
arguments that RBP’s lack of locational constraints renders it unjust and unreasonable. The 
Order finds that “the volume of capacity that PJM will procure through the RBP auction—
up to 6,831 MW—is relatively small compared with total existing supply in PJM (149 
[gigawatts (GW)]), so even if RBP Resources are not located in the exact same Locational 
Deliverability Areas [(LDAs)] as new loads, the effect of any locational constraints should 
be limited.”14 But downplaying the capacity volumes, in this context, cannot be squared 
with the Order’s premise that a BRA shortfall of the same magnitude is a dire reliability 
crisis.15 Nor does the Order explain why the absence of locational constraints in the RBP 
is immaterial when (1) the Commission’s acceptance of the BRA structure was predicated

13 RBP Order P 63 & n.90 (citing JCA Protest at 16). 
14 Id. P 97. 
15 Id. PP 3, 5.

- 5 - 
 
upon the inclusion of locational constraints; and (2) history shows that zonal capacity price 
separation can increase costs to ratepayers by hundreds of millions of dollars. The RBP 
resources selected without regard to location may not serve the reliability needs of the 
zones where load growth is expected. And under RBP, those resources will participate in 
the BRA as price takers and will thereby diminish the effect of the BRA’s locational price 
signals for up to 15 years. The Commission cannot dismiss the concerns of Joint Consumer 
Advocates (and others) that the RBP’s lack of locational constraints risks burdening 
ratepayers with additional capacity, transmission and energy costs that could otherwise be 
avoided based on the unsubstantiated and vague contention that such costs will be limited.16 
For the above reasons, and as explained in greater detail in Part II of this filing, 
below, Joint Consumer Advocates respectfully request that the Commission (1) grant 
rehearing of the RBP Order; (2) find unjust and unreasonable the four elements of the RBP 
framework identified herein by Joint Consumer Advocates; and (3) direct PJM to 
incorporate changes to those elements in any subsequent FPA section 20517 filing PJM 
proposes.   
I. 
STATEMENT OF ISSUES AND SPECIFICATION OF ERRORS 
In accordance with Commission Rules of Practice and Procedure 713(c)(1) and 
(c)(2),18 the Joint Consumer Advocates provide the following enumerated statement of 
issues and specification of errors, including citations to representative Commission and 
court precedent on which they rely:  
1. The RBP Order errs as a matter of law and is arbitrary and capricious and not based in 
substantial evidence in accepting a market-based rate auction structure that exceeds the 
 
16 JCA Protest at 29.  
17 16 U.S.C. § 824d. 
18 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.713(c)(1)-(2).

- 6 - 
 
Commission’s statutory authority and is unjust and unreasonable because it permits the 
unmitigated exercise of seller side market power. PJM has admitted, and the Order 
finds, that pursuant to the RBP’s pay-as-bid structure, sellers are more likely to offer 
the expected clearing price than their marginal costs. Accordingly, the RBP 
procurement is unlikely to produce competition between sellers based upon their 
marginal costs of production and will result instead in unjust and unreasonable rates 
that reflect the exercise of seller-side market power and resource offers that game the 
RBP’s market price cap. The Commission seeks to defend RBP based upon the number 
of potential sellers, but a large number of uncompetitive offers is not the same as 
competition. Without incentives for sellers to offer at prices approximating their costs, 
there is no reason to expect this auction structure to yield a just and reasonable rate that 
approximates what would be produced by fair competition based on the marginal 
production costs of the resources bidding into the market.19   
2. The RBP Order errs as a matter of law and is arbitrary and capricious and not based in 
substantial evidence by accepting a market-based price cap of $555/MW-day absent 
evidence that this cap is just and reasonable for the long-term product being procured 
and appropriately reflects the financing and other costs minus the expected revenue 
streams of resources that will provide capacity in response to RBP (not BRA) price 
signals. The RBP Order fails to provide a reasoned explanation based on the record 
evidence for accepting an average-weighted $555/MW-day price cap. Instead, it 
arbitrarily and capriciously relies upon the market price cap at which resources would 
have cleared in the 2028/2029 BRA (but for the imposition of a price collar), even 
though the BRA and RBP auction designs are fundamentally dissimilar in numerous 
material respects.20 
3. The RBP Order errs as a matter of law and is arbitrary and capricious in failing to 
respond to Joint Consumer Advocates’ objection that it is unjust and unreasonable to 
require ratepayers to pay for 15-year procurements when there is uncontroverted record 
evidence that 5-year procurements are sufficient to meet PJM’s needs and RBP’s 
purpose of satisfying a near-term resource adequacy shortfall. RBP’s acquisition of 15-
year capacity commitments is unjust and unreasonable because it may increase 
ratepayer acquisition costs by as much as $13 billion for no justifiable purpose and 
without any commensurate consumer benefit.21

4. The RBP Order errs as a matter of law and is arbitrary and capricious and is unjust and 
unreasonable in accepting an RBP procurement structure that does not incorporate 
locational constraints for offering resources. This constitutes an impermissible 
departure from the Commission’s approval of the BRA (which required such 
constraints), is not reasoned decision making, and is likely to result in excessive 
capacity costs due to the non-deliverability of the resources to areas of need, related 
and unnecessary increases in energy and transmission costs, and the acquisition of 
resources not suited to meet the region’s reliability needs.22  
II. 
REQUEST FOR REHEARING 
A. 
The Commission’s approval of RBP exceeds its authority to rely 
on competition to set just and reasonable market-based rates 
because RBP permits and incents the exercise of seller-side market 
power. 
The RBP Order finds that PJM’s “pay-as-bid”23 auction “process for selecting RBP 
Resources . . .  [is] just and reasonable.”24 The Order accepts this pay-as-bid approach 
despite RBP’s “lack of direct market power screens or mitigation.”25 The Commission’s 
determination is unsustainable because the RBP’s pay-as-bid resource selection process 
permits—and will likely result in—the unmitigated exercise of seller-side market power. 
In “a pay-as-bid procurement [such as RBP] each selected resource is compensated 
based on its individual offer rather than a market-clearing price established by the marginal 
resource.”26 As proposed, RBP nowhere requires sellers to bid their own production costs 
and nothing prevents them from “offer[ing] the expected clearing price” of $555/MW-

24 RBP Order P 74.

day.27 Indeed, PJM’s own supporting witness concedes that, “[i]n a pay-as-bid approach, 
unlike a uniform clearing price construct where sellers are expected to offer a marginal 
cost, sellers are more likely to offer the expected clearing price.”28 The academic and 
regulatory literature is to like effect: “pay-as-bid auctions create the incentive for all 
suppliers to bid the expected market-clearing price, rather than submitting bids reflecting 
each facility’s individual marginal costs.”29  Tellingly, the Order agrees: “as both PJM and 
protesters note, sellers are theoretically less likely to offer near their marginal costs in a 
pay-as-bid auction.”30 
The Commission’s approval of RBP violates basic tenets governing the use of 
competitive procurement to set just and reasonable rates under the FPA. The Supreme 
Court has held that “the Commission lacks the authority to place exclusive reliance on 
market prices,”31 explaining that the “prevailing price in the marketplace cannot be the 
final measure of ‘just and reasonable’ rates mandated by the [FPA].”32 The Supreme Court 
has also found that the “directives contained in [sections] 205 [and] 206,” to ensure the 
justness and reasonableness of any sale of electric energy for resale in interstate commerce,

include the “responsibility to consider . . . the anticompetitive effects of regulated aspects 
of interstate utility operations.”33 Accordingly, and as the D.C. Circuit has explained, it is 
only “when there is a competitive market [that] [the Commission] may rely upon market-
based prices in lieu of cost-of-service regulation to assure a ‘just and reasonable’ result.”34 
In other words, market-based procurement is not an end in itself, but is permissible only in 
circumstances that make it “rational to assume” that competition will produce a price “close 
to marginal cost, such that the seller makes only a normal return on its investment.”35 
The Order does not identify, nor does the record contain, supporting evidence 
making it reasonable to assume that the resulting RBP procurement prices will be the result 
of true price competition or will reflect the marginal cost of the resources to be procured. 
The Order cites no judicial or Commission precedent in support of its approval of RBP as 
a pay-as-bid auction36 where sellers “are . . . likely to offer the expected clearing price” as 
opposed to their marginal cost.37 The Order does not address Joint Consumer Advocates’ 
objection that the RBP is an unlawful market-based rate when measured against the 
standards of Texaco, Elizabethtown, and their progeny.38 While the Order dismisses these 
objections to RBP as “theoretical,” it is beyond purview that sound economic theory

predictive of anticompetitive behavior is centrally relevant to the Commission’s exercise 
of its ratemaking authority to ensure just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory 
rates.39 The Order fails to demonstrate that RBP will be a fair and competitive procurement 
process free of the exercise of seller-side market power.40 
RBP’s shortcomings are manifest when compared against PJM’s standard auction 
capacity procurement mechanism, the BRA. In contrast to the RBP, “the objective of [the 
BRA is] to procure the least-cost, competitively-priced combination of resources necessary 
to meet the region’s reliability objectives.”41 The Commission has found the BRA design 
to be just and reasonable because it is intended to ensure competition and mitigate seller-
side market power by myriad means.42 The BRA includes must-offer resource obligations, 
market seller resource offer caps, a market price cap, and oversight of bids/bidding by the 
Independent Market Monitor (IMM), designed to discipline seller-side market power.43 A 
central premise of the design is that capacity sellers are expected to bid their own marginal 
costs. In accepting the BRA construct and its single clearing price model, the Commission

N.Y. v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1 (2002).

present competitive or just and reasonable. As a subset of the Joint Consumer Advocates have shown in their 
pending complaint in FERC Docket No. EL25-18-000, there is inadequate new entry to mitigate the market

RPM/BRA structure.

found that “under this model, the generator has the proper incentive to bid the lowest price 
that covers its marginal cost.”44 
The RBP includes none of the BRA’s approved mitigation measures. In something 
of an understatement, the Order acknowledges that RBP “lack[s] . . . direct market power 
screens or mitigation.”45  In fact, there is nothing in the approved design that requires RBP 
sellers to bid their own production costs and nothing that prevents them from “offer[ing] 
the expected clearing price.”46 A seller’s ability to bid successfully unconstrained by its 
competitors’ cost of production is a paradigmatic example of the exercise of seller-side 
market power.47 Here, every resource eligible to offer into the RBP can bid to raise prices 
to the $555/MW-day average-price cap regardless of its marginal cost or that of its 
competitors. In short, resources bidding into the RBP will be engaged in a gaming strategy 
rather than price competition. 
The Order proffers a series of assertions purporting to show that the RBP construct 
is just and reasonable and “the exercise of market power is unlikely.”48 None are 
convincing.

First, the Order dismisses the “theoretical drawback” of sellers offering the 
expected clearing price as opposed to their marginal costs of production based upon “the 
Charles River Associates Survey Results indicating strong seller interest in the RBP 
auction.”49 Even if true, this is a legally insufficient response. The Supreme Court has held 
that Commission cannot rely upon competition alone as the basis for finding the RBP just 
and reasonable.50 That is particularly true here, where the design of the “market” facilitates 
uncompetitive conduct. 
The Order’s dismissal of market power concerns rests entirely upon a single 
assertion in PJM’s transmittal filing that “the exercise of market power is unlikely if even 
a portion of the more than 130 GW of supply identified in the Charles River Associates 
Survey Results decides to participate and drive down prices.”51 But this is pure surmise 
and is contradicted by PJM’s own statement two pages later that bidders are “more likely 
to offer the expected clearing price.”52 A collection of uncompetitive offers, no matter how 
numerous, does not constitute competition capable of producing just and reasonable prices. 
Moreover, any supposition that the number of potential suppliers will drive down 
offer prices, because suppliers will want to make sure their offers clear, ignores other

aspects of the RBP auction structure. The RBP, as proposed, does not clear resources 
strictly in offer price order. Rather, it prioritizes offers for resources that can interconnect 
and become commercially operational quickly—a significantly more limited set of 
resources.53 According to the CRA presentation, most potential supply resources are still 
in the early permitting stages and are targeting commercial operation dates in the early 
2030s.54 Only about 80 projects had anticipated commercial operation dates from 2026 
through 2029, compared to more than 260 from 2030  through 2033.55 So, even if these 
forecasts are correct, they demonstrate that resources that can be built quickly will be in 
short supply. And because the RBP includes no resource offer caps, suppliers may offer 
those resources at prices well above $555/MW-day and still be confident of clearing if 
other resources offer at prices below $555/MW-day.

RFI data to claim that the RBP will function as a competitive solicitation. One of PJM’s 
witnesses alleged that the RFI’s identification of a “large set of potential supply to 
participate in the RBP . . . allows the RBP to function more like a competitive

with the data center would pay the maximum price for 
capacity (shortage pricing). 
 
* * * 
 
Under the RBP Filing, a data center load in [Baltimore Gas 
& Electric (BGE)] would be allowed to procure capacity 
located in a distant LDA, e.g. [Commonwealth Edison 
Company (ComEd)]. BGE, located within the [Southwest 
Mid-Atlantic Area Council (SWMAAC)] LDA has been one 
of the constrained LDAs in PJM. In this scenario, BGE 
LDA’s load would increase without offsetting generation 
and without additional transmission capacity to import 
power from outside BGE under emergency conditions. In 
this scenario, BGE’s reliability requirement would not be

115 Id. 
116 IMM Answer at 27-28.

- 30 - 
 
satisfied and BGE customers would pay the maximum price 
for capacity as a result. 
 
Allowing capacity and load to be added without accounting 
for locational resource adequacy would also result in higher 
energy market prices and increased transmission costs. In the 
example, in the BGE LDA with higher load and lack of 
offsetting generation and transmission capacity to import 
power would result in higher prices in the energy market. 
This would trigger transmission upgrades. 
    
The Order wrongly dismisses these concerns in the RBP context even as it treated 
parallel concerns as significant to the BRA and as a reason to reject PJM’s IRAS proposal. 
The Order’s refusal to require locational procurement constraints in the RBP is thus an 
unexplained departure from precedent.117 While the IRAS decision postdates the RBP 
Order, the Commission on rehearing must explain why it dismissed the concern in the RBP 
context while crediting it in the IRAS context. 
The Order gestures at an argument that locational requirements are not needed 
because the RBP responds to an aggregate resource adequacy deficiency, not location-
specific needs. According to the Order, “the RBP is designed to address the PJM Region’s 
capacity shortfall, such that it is addressing an effectively region-wide problem.”118 But 
even assuming arguendo that this is correct, the Order’s failure to impose RBP locational 
constraints cannot be reconciled with the inclusion of locational constraints in the modeling 
for PJM’s RPM, which is likewise a region-wide procurement to ensure resource adequacy.  
Moreover, the Order’s characterization of RBP as responsive to aggregate region-
wide load growth is contrary to PJM’s characterization of its proposal, which makes crystal 
 
117 Encino Motorcars, LLC, 579 U.S. at 212-13. 
118 RBP Order P 97.

- 31 - 
 
clear that RBP is intended to address the enormous amount of projected load growth from 
new data centers that is outpacing new supply.119 
PJM hosts the largest concentration of data center load in the 
world.s “PJM’s load forecast predicts peak load growth of 
32 gigawatts [(“GW”)] from 2024 to 2030, 30 GW of which 
is projected to be from data centers.” Year-over-year, the 
shortfall of capacity supply needed to meet demand (plus a 
reasonable reserve margin) has grown despite a net increase 
of 1,294.4 MW Installed Capacity (“ICAP”) of supply 
between the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 BRA. In other words, 
the addition of new supply has not kept pace with rapid large 
load demand growth, thus giving rise to the significant 
tightening of the capacity market in recent years and the 
subsequent resource adequacy shortfalls. To mitigate the 
potential reliability risks associated with resource adequacy 
shortfalls, PJM is proposing this RBP as a one-time, 
supplementary mechanism to procure additional supply to 
meet the resource adequacy needs of the PJM Region. 
And there is nothing mysterious about the locations of this load growth. Everyone knows 
where the new data center load has materialized within PJM and where it is projected to 
grow. And the RBP, in responding to this new large load growth, is addressing even more 
concentrated, location-specific load growth than the BRA generally does. If anything, the 
RBP context makes locational considerations more, not less, important, than they are in the 
BRA—a reality recognized by PJM’s proposal to allocate RBP costs to zones based on 
their large load forecasts.120  
The Order’s apparent contention that RBP is necessary to meet diverse aggregate 
region-wide load growth cannot be reconciled with its own statements to the contrary and 
the record evidence. The Commission accepts RBP, in part, because “PJM’s ordinary

- 32 - 
 
instrument for procuring sufficient capacity to meet PJM’s reliability requirement, the 
RPM, has failed to keep pace with the unprecedented influx of large load into the PJM 
region in recent years.”121 In excusing RBP’s lack of locational constraints, the Order 
apparently ignores the transparent and compelling evidence that PJM’s resource adequacy 
shortfall is driven by new data center load and that load growth is projected to occur in 
specific zones within PJM. The Order itself states that “[t]he largest driver of the shortfall 
was 5,250 MW of load growth forecast for [the 2027/2028 Delivery Year], nearly 5,100 
MW of which was due to data centers.”122 The IMM has found that it is new data center 
load that is the causal driver of increased capacity prices within PJM.123 
While data center growth has occurred over five or more 
years, PJM has failed to address the impact of data centers 
on the PJM Capacity Market over the last four capacity 
auctions. PJM has made its RBP Filing only under direct 
pressure from the Commission and the White House and the 
PJM governors, among others. It is clear that the current 
situation and the current tariff in PJM are untenable and 
therefore unjust and unreasonable. The addition of data 
center load has resulted in adding $29.4 billion to the cost of 
capacity, higher energy costs, higher transmission costs, and 
a significant degradation of system reliability. 
 
The White House’s National Energy Dominance Council’s Statement of Principles 
Regarding PJM likewise points to new data center load as the causal driver of PJM’s 
resource adequacy needs and provides that “PJM should allocate the cost of any new 
capacity procured through the aforementioned Reliability Backstop Auction to load serving

entities (LSEs) with new data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed 
to be curtailable.”124 
  Contrary to the Order’s determination that the resource adequacy problem is 
region-wide, PJM has provided uncontroverted record evidence of the zones where new 
large loads are projected.125 Indeed, the Order recognizes the zonal nature of the problem 
in observing that126 
it may be just and reasonable for PJM to allocate RBP costs 
based on updated load forecast information. PJM could base 
the RBP allocation on the difference between the actual load 
for 2026/2027 delivery year in each Electric Distributor 
zone/area with the most recent 2028/2029 delivery year load 
forecast for each Electric Distributor zone/area. 
Finally, the Order seeks to defend the absence of locational constraints based on 
the “reasonabl[e] assum[ption] that RBP Resources will include anticipated Network 
Upgrade costs in their RBP Sell Offers.”127 This assumption is unfounded and stands 
reality on its head. Because RBP has no locational constraints, offering resources can bid 
regardless of where they are located and, in doing so, seek to avoid Network Upgrade 
costs—without regard to whether siting in that location will materially aid PJM in serving 
new large loads. Indeed, it is in the economic self-interest of offering resources to do so. 
Plainly, the Commission seeks to have PJM pay generators regardless of where they are 
located, with no assurance that these resources will meet the resource adequacy needs of 
LDAs with forecasted new large loads, while knowing that the failure to impose locational

request that the Commission: (1) grant rehearing of the RBP Order; (2) find unjust and 
unreasonable the four elements of the RBP framework identified herein by Joint Consumer

FPA section 205 filing PJM proposes.

sections.title: I. Statement of Issues and Specification of errors

A. The Commission’s approval of RBP exceeds its authority to rely on competition to set just and reasonable market-based rates because RBP permits and incents the exercise of seller-side market power.
B. The Order provides no reasoned explanation for approving PJM’s proposed $555/MW-day price cap.
C. The Order is arbitrary and capricious in failing to address why it requires 15-year RBP resource commitments when PJM admits that 5-year contracts eliminate the need for RBP procurement.
D. The RBP Order errs by failing to require that the RBP incorporate locational constraints.
